$comment: Bauhaus type direction. Fonts come from foundations/typography/source/pairings.json; this file says which suit this approach and how to set them, and proposes new Google Fonts pairings. Sizes are rules of thumb unless a source is given.
character: Geometric and grotesque sans-serifs, built from circle, square and straight stroke, set bold, large and asymmetric on a grid. Type is structure: it sits on bars, runs up edges and balances the forms. Lowercase was the Bauhaus's own experiment (Bayer's single alphabet); sentence case is the everyday default.

anatomy.$comment: What to look for when judging a typeface for this approach.

construction.want: Geometric: round o, c, e close to circles; straight, even stems
construction.why: Echoes the circle-square-triangle vocabulary; Bayer's universal alphabet was built from arcs, angles and straight lines.

strokes.why: Matches the even weight of bars and rules.

terminals.why: Echoes square corners; rounded terminals soften the construction.

apertures.why: Pure geometric faces close up at small sizes; the body face needs enough opening to read at 9-14 pt.

xHeight.want: Moderate (geometric) for display, taller for body
xHeight.why: Geometric display faces often have small x-heights; the body face must still read on phones.

weights.want: A true bold or black for headlines
weights.why: Headline stems should approach the medium bar weight (2% of the short side).

avoid: Serifs and slab serifs for headlines
Calligraphic, humanist or rounded sans for display
Novelty 'Bauhaus' display faces (ITC Bauhaus, stencil pastiche)

fit.$comment: core = recommended, good = works, accent = special cases, avoid = not for this approach.

schibsted.why: Sturdy neo-grotesque with a heavy 800-900 for bar-weight headlines; one family keeps hierarchy to size and weight, as in Bauhaus print set in jobbing grotesques.

bricolage-figtree.why: Bricolage at 800 is a heavy grotesque that holds its own beside bars; Figtree's geometric body fits. Its slightly irregular details are less strict than the style wants.

plex.why: IBM Plex Sans and Mono suit the engineered precision, but the pairing's display face is a serif; use only for technical products, with Plex Sans Bold for headlines if the product agrees.

source.why: Source Sans 3 is clear but humanist and the display face is a serif; use only for text-heavy products that need the layout rules more than the look.

instrument.why: A condensed, high-contrast serif headline is the opposite of geometric, monolinear construction.

young-onest.why: Soft, heavy serif; too warm and rounded for exact geometry.

nunito.why: Rounded terminals contradict square corners and cut bars.

alegreya.why: Calligraphic letterforms bring the pen back in; the Bauhaus took it out.

fraunces-commissioner.why: Soft, wonky serif charm works against precision.

newPairings.name: Geometric Constructivist
newPairings.mood: Clean, constructed and calm. One geometric family inspired by 1920s German sans-serifs, used bold for headlines and regular for text: hierarchy from size and weight alone.
newPairings.bestFor: Bauhaus-style posters, architecture, furniture, design studios, culture, education.

display.case: Sentence case, or all lowercase for headlines
display.notes: Described by its designer as inspired by the 1920s German sans-serifs; an original interpretation in the Futura tradition, not a copy. Variable since version 3.0.

body.notes: Small x-height for a text face: set body one step larger than with a grotesque (17-18 px on screen).

newPairings.name: Heavy Geometric
newPairings.mood: Loud and direct. A heavy early-20th-century geometric sans for headlines over Jost for text. For posters that need to be read from across a room.
newPairings.bestFor: Events, posters, signage, campaigns with one big message.

display.case: Sentence case, or all lowercase for headlines
display.designer: Matt Bailey and Tyler Finck (The League of Moveable Type)
display.notes: Based on Matt Bailey's Spartan, itself based on early 20th-century American geometric sans-serifs (ATF Spartan). Variable since 2020.

handwritten.$comment: Handwritten accent faces from foundations/typography/source/handwritten.json. use: none | accent (one short element) | core (part of the style). A product picks one in brand.json -> typography.hand.
handwritten.why: The style is built from type as geometry: grotesques, circles, squares and bars. A hand face breaks its machine logic.

typeWithArt.weightMatch: Headline stems close to the medium bar (2% of the short side) at headline size; heavy bars (4%) sit above or below the headline, never thinner than its stems.
typeWithArt.scaleMatch: Headline cap height between 1/4 and 1/2 of the focal form's diameter, so the form leads and the type answers.
typeWithArt.alignment: Left edges of text blocks sit on column lines; baselines on the 4-unit baseline grid. Type may sit directly on a bar (bar below the baseline) or run up a vertical bar.
typeWithArt.spacing: At least one margin (6%) between type and a form, unless the type deliberately overlaps a solid bar or ground.

sizes.$comment: Headline cap height as a share of the canvas height, and body text minimums. Rules of thumb; Bauhaus headlines run larger than Humanist Minimal's.
sizes.viewingDistance: Sign-industry rule of thumb: about 1 inch (25 mm) of letter height for every 10 feet (3 m) of viewing distance for basic legibility; double it for comfortable reading.

measure.source: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (45-75); slightly shorter here to fit narrow grid columns

setting.case: Sentence case by default. All-lowercase headlines are allowed for the whole product (decide once, in the brand, not per piece). Capitals only for labels of one to three words and vertical edge labels.
setting.rotation: Text runs at 0° or -90° (bottom to top). Never on the 45° diagonal for more than three words.
setting.rag: Ragged right; no justified text; no centred text.
setting.numbers: Large numerals can be the image (dates, prices); use the mono for small data.

rules: Geometric or grotesque sans, bold headlines, monolinear strokes.
Three sizes and two weights per piece, with big jumps between sizes.
Left-aligned on the grid; text may turn 90° up an edge.
Sentence case or all lowercase, never all caps for headlines.
No serifs, scripts, rounded or novelty 'Bauhaus' fonts.
